description: We are Team Seven Nova, a group of students interested in systems engineering, programming, and mathematical modeling. We aim to build innovative software solutions for space exploration challenges.
summary:
Planning a mission to the Moon’s south pole begins with two deceptively simple questions: Will there be enough sunlight to generate power, and will the spacecraft be able to communicate with Earth?

At the lunar poles, the answers can change dramatically with location, terrain, and time. Even a nearby ridge can make a difference.

Our team, Seven Nova, developed **LUNA VISION**, an interactive, bilingual web application designed to make these challenges easier to explore. The platform brings together lunar landing-region coordinates, visualization tools, and a reproducible scientific pipeline for evaluating sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility using NASA's open resources.

Users can explore 13 documented lunar south-pole regions, examine geographic conditions, and work toward comparing mission opportunities across different dates. The application includes terrain-aware computational methods, data visualization, and export tools.

Our prototype currently incorporates NASA-published site coordinates, while full terrain-corrected results require processing additional LOLA and JPL SPICE datasets.

We believe lunar exploration tools should be scientifically transparent, accessible, and understandable—not limited to specialists.
details:
LUNA VISION — Finding Light and Connection at the Lunar South Pole

Team: Seven Nova
Challenge: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser
Tagline: Find the light. Keep the connection.

The Challenge We Wanted to Solve

The Moon's south pole is one of the most promising—and demanding—destinations for future exploration.

Unlike Earth, where the Sun rises high above the horizon in many locations, sunlight near the lunar poles often arrives at very low angles. Mountains and crater rims can block solar illumination. The Earth can also disappear behind the local horizon, interrupting direct communication.

For a lunar mission, these conditions matter enormously. A landing site that offers favorable sunlight may not provide equally favorable communication windows.

We wanted to make these trade-offs easier to explore without requiring users to navigate several specialized scientific applications.

Our Solution

LUNA VISION is a browser-based lunar exploration and mission-analysis platform.

It is designed to bring together information about lunar surface topography, solar illumination, and Earth visibility in one interactive environment.

Instead of treating every landing location as a point on an ideal, flat surface, our approach examines how the surrounding landscape can affect what an observer sees in the sky.

The application provides a practical starting point for exploring 13 lunar south-pole regions documented in NASA's Lunar Surface Data Book.

How LUNA VISION Works

1. Exploring Lunar Regions

Users can select documented lunar south-pole regions through an interactive interface. The application uses published NASA coordinates to identify each region.

2. Understanding the Terrain

We developed a processing pipeline intended to use NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation products.

The algorithm samples the landscape in different directions to construct a local horizon profile. It accounts for the Moon's curvature, observer height, and incomplete elevation coverage.

Processed terrain can be displayed in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional views.

3. Tracking the Sun and Earth

Our computational pipeline uses NASA/JPL SPICE resources to calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to a lunar observer.

These positions can then be compared against the terrain horizon to estimate solar visibility and geometric direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

4. Comparing Mission Conditions

The system is designed to compare regions and observation periods according to solar exposure, Earth visibility, possible communication interruptions, and simultaneous illumination-and-communication windows.

A simplified solar-power calculator also allows users to explore how panel area and efficiency influence estimated generation potential.

5. Making the Results Accessible

The interface supports English and Arabic, interactive visualizations, and downloadable CSV and JSON reports. It can be explored through a web browser without specialized mission-planning software.

What Makes Our Approach Different?

Our main contribution is not a new lunar dataset. It is an accessible framework that connects open planetary data, computational geometry, and a practical decision-support interface.

We focused on three principles:

  • Transparency: The application distinguishes measured inputs, derived calculations, and unavailable information.
  • Reproducibility: The data-processing and analysis code can be inspected, tested, and extended.
  • Accessibility: Scientific information is presented through an interface designed for students, educators, researchers, and mission-planning teams.

We also consider scientific uncertainty part of the interface rather than something to hide. Missing terrain information is not automatically classified as visible sky or blocked sky.

Technologies and Scientific Resources

We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python to build the interface and computational pipeline.

The scientific architecture incorporates methods for processing lunar elevation rasters, transforming astronomical reference frames, calculating local azimuth and elevation, and evaluating geometric visibility.

The implementation uses tools and libraries including NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, SciPy, and SpiceyPy, together with automated testing and a GitHub Actions data-processing workflow.

Development and Validation

We implemented the interactive application, prepared a reproducible NASA-data-processing pipeline, and performed 21 automated numerical and functional checks using controlled test inputs.

These tests support the internal behavior of the algorithms, including terrain sampling, lunar curvature, visibility classification, and missing-data handling.

However, the current submission package does not contain the complete downloaded LOLA elevation datasets or processed JPL SPICE results. Full terrain-corrected analysis and independent validation against official ephemeris results remain necessary.

For this reason, LUNA VISION is presented as a research and educational prototype, not a flight-qualified landing-site selection system.

Expected Impact

We believe the next generation of lunar exploration will benefit from tools that make complex scientific information easier to understand and evaluate.

LUNA VISION aims to help students discover how lunar geography influences exploration, support researchers in preliminary scenario analysis, and provide a foundation for more advanced scientific decision-support systems.

Our long-term vision is to extend the platform with higher-resolution terrain products, improved uncertainty analysis, verified astronomical calculations, and more realistic spacecraft power and communication models.

LUNA VISION begins with a simple idea: choosing where to land should also mean understanding when the Sun—and the Earth—will be visible.
